overview: This regional record spans late Ahom kingship, Burmese intervention and British colonial expansion, not one unchanged state. Its 1783 to 1800 outline is misplaced over Bhutan and excludes the Ahom heartland; coverage is absent from 1800 to 1815. The later outline overreaches into neighboring hill regions and does not establish common rule everywhere. The much earlier kingdom of Kamarupa has its own history.

periods.title: Late Ahom struggles
periods.summary: Rebellion and rival claims weakened royal power around the capital at Jorhat.

periods.title: Burmese predominance
periods.summary: Burmese intervention subordinated Ahom rulers before war with the East India Company.

periods.title: Uneven British expansion
periods.summary: Purandar Singha briefly ruled part of Upper Assam as a tributary before annexation.

periods.title: Colonial province and plantations
periods.summary: Assam became a separate Chief Commissionership in 1874; colonial rule continued beyond this map window.

sections.title: A kingdom’s final decades and a changing province

items.text: The struggle for Assam involved competing Ahom claimants and Burmese armies. In 1819 Purandar Singha fled while Chandrakanta Singha became a nominal ruler under Burmese power. By 1822 another claimant, Jogeswar Singha, served as a Burmese vassal. A king’s title no longer guaranteed control.

The 1826 Treaty of Yandabo required Burma to abandon its claims to Assam. British rule developed unevenly: Purandar regained part of Upper Assam as a tributary in 1833, but the Company annexed his territory in September 1838.

Jorhat’s timeline records Maniram Baruah writing Buranji Vivek Ratna in 1838. Buranjis preserved political memory in chronicle form. The same timeline records the Company opening Purandar’s burial mound in 1847: surviving history includes intrusive colonial investigation as well as written records.

At Charaideo, ninety royal burial mounds survive within the protected necropolis. Built across the thirteenth to nineteenth centuries, they are inherited Ahom heritage rather than ninety creations of this map period. Hollow chambers lie beneath earth mounds, with shrines above and octagonal enclosing walls.

The cemetery was a carefully shaped landscape. People planted sacred trees, including trees used for coffins and bark manuscripts, and directed streams into water bodies. Me-Dam Me-Phi ancestor rituals continue there. Trees could belong to the worlds of books, burials and living memory at once.

In his 1837 account, physician John M’Cosh described most Guwahati houses as bamboo and matting structures, while some officials occupied masonry houses. The town’s homes differed visibly with materials and status.

M’Cosh described canoe transport and builders joining two canoes with crossbeams to carry bulky cotton or straw. One trunk could become a boat; two boats could become a floating platform. Paddles and poles supplied the power.

His agricultural account describes rice seedlings moved from manured nursery plots into ploughed, flooded fields. Mustard also supplied oil and an export crop. Food production required knowledge of water, soil and planting seasons.

He also recorded women weaving silk within families, with wealthier households owning three to six looms. His description includes several kinds of silk and different silkworm foods. Making cloth was skilled household production.

A modern museum account traces weaving through wedding songs, lullabies and folktales, and describes skills passing from parents to children and mentors to apprentices. This continuing tradition helps explain why textiles belong to family memory as well as museum displays; it cannot date every song to Ahom times.

sections.title: Tea, migration and difficult working lives

items.text: By 1872 Assam Valley plantations produced about six million pounds of tea. British capital and overseas markets drove expansion. From the mid-1860s, indenture contracts brought workers from other parts of India and restricted their ability to leave after arrival. The familiar drink depended on an unequal labor system.

Recruiters sometimes promised prosperity that plantation life failed to deliver. The university’s history describes inadequate food, unhygienic lodging and limited medical facilities. Boats and steamers carried migrants upriver, with regular service to Dibrugarh from 1860. These were working communities enduring hardship, not simply numbers in tea-export tables.

sections.title: Care, classrooms and a page of astronomy

items.text: M’Cosh reported treating prisoners with scurvy at Guwahati by buying baskets of oranges and lemons from the market when hospital supplies were inadequate. His 1837 account connects illness with prison conditions and access to food, without proving that everyone received comparable care.

The Baptist mission’s own history reports a girls’ school building at Guwahati in 1849. It also describes young people organizing a school and sending a group to ask for books and a teacher. Mission schools promoted Christianity, but the account also reveals local demand for learning.

The February 1846 Orunodoi explained the solar system and compared Earth’s shape with a pomelo. Readers encountered astronomy in Assamese alongside religious material and news. Its list of seven principal planets belongs to the knowledge presented at that moment. Even a fruit could help explain a planet.

Assamese: “গ্ৰহৰ বিবৰন” (grahar bibaran), paired with “The Solar System” in the February 1846 Orunodoi. The heading literally concerns a description of the planets. This is the spelling in the digital transcription of the periodical, with a simplified Roman transliteration; it represents one printed Assamese text, not every language spoken in Assam.

sections.title: How we can investigate this period

items.text: Assam State Archives preserves eight correspondence series covering 1823 to 1874, connecting the Governor-General’s agent, district officers and the Bengal government. These records can help reconstruct how colonial decisions were made. They preserve administrators’ viewpoints, so historians also need local chronicles, material remains and other voices.

ending.text: The 1838 annexation ended Purandar’s restored kingship, not Assam’s communities. Colonial administration continued beyond 1878, and Assam later became part of independent India.
